title: Sana and the Bloom
markdown:
The Riverside Conservatory’s annual exhibition was a dazzling explosion of colour against a sky that looked like a grumpy old badger. For Sana the wolf, trainee botanist whose fur was always a bit of a mess, as if she had just wrestled a particularly ticklish hedge, it felt like standing on the very edge of a very big wobble. She was in charge of the Bloom of Tranquility. Not a run-of-the-mill plant: the prize bloom, jewel in the Conservatory’s crown, the sort of flower that made people gasp and point and generally feel very impressed.

Madame Evangeline, director, voice like tiny well-oiled sleigh bells, had waved a hand that might have been a butterfly taking off. “Keep an eye on it, dear. Ever so precious.” Sana managed a wobbly nod. Her heart flamencoed. Her mind had become a noisy theme park of disasters on repeat. The deepest secret was a fear of not being good enough, which turned her into a stiff awkward statue.

Kit the dormouse, lab partner small enough for a thimble, scurried onto her shoulder. Whiskers twitched. “It looks quite happy. Perhaps a tiny bit more lumina-dew?”

Startled by the miniature weight, she fumbled the glass vial. It pirouetted, clink-clink-clinked the display table, and puffed a shy pearly cloud. Kit squeaked. Sana froze. The Big Mess, beginning. The Bloom received only a faint shimmer, but the near-miss shivered through her. She smoothed fur, trying to look expert. “A little atmospheric tweak.” Inside, somersaults.

Later, seeking refuge at the Riverside Café of Effortless Charm, she nursed lukewarm chamomile. Plants tumbled from every surface; the air buzzed with the almost conspiratorial clink of cups. The place looked as if it had not tried at all, and Sana suspected it had spent ages getting that thrown-together look just right. Artists and thinkers drifted through as if they had simply materialized, perfectly at ease, while she sat like a statue that had forgotten its plinth.

“I cannot believe I nearly dropped the lumina-dew,” she confessed while Kit diligently worked a dropped scone crumb, tiny paws sugared. “Madame Evangeline will have my tail. Or, worse, the compost heap. The compost heap.”

Kit looked up, earnest. “You did not spill it all. And you stopped it. That was quick thinking.”

She blinked. Quick thinking? She had felt like a clumsy giant. His gaze held a peculiar unwavering belief. As she sipped, her eyes drifted to the bicycles parked outside. A recent shower had left them gleaming, each catching sunlight in little flashes. A small quiet sight: order finding its way after bother. A tiny spark of something hopeful flickered.

Next morning the Bloom looked less tranquil than unwell. Petals drooped, edges jaundiced, apologizing for decay. Tomorrow’s opening ticked in her skull. “Wilting. I do not know what it needs.”

Professor Grumbleweed shuffled over, a man whose frown seemed permanently glued, and peered at the sad bloom with a sigh like a rusty door. “A shame. Such a delicate thing. Perhaps it is simply a bit too much for less experienced hands.” The words wore a cloak of concern and landed like tiny sharp pebbles on Sana’s already bruised ego. The familiar suffocating urge to retreat, to hand the bloom to anyone who seemed more capable, washed over her.

Later Madame Evangeline appeared, usual cheer replaced by worry. “Sana, dear. Are you quite sure you are managing? If not, young Tegid is all ready to step in. He has quite a knack for theatrics.” The choice was stark: cling to shaky confidence, or admit fear and let Tegid—whose theatrics Sana suspected involved far more glitter than gardening—take over. Faced with his potential appointment she faltered, then mumbled that she was perfectly fine, a decision that felt less like bravery than a desperate attempt to outrun her own anxious thoughts.

Then the sky threw a tantrum. Rain lashed the Conservatory’s magnificent glass domes with a furious relentless drumming. The Bloom, already stressed and weak, quivered. Water it desperately needed became an overwhelming destructive torrent. A cold dread washed over Sana, different this time: not only reputation, but the fragile life hanging in the balance.

Kit, perched precariously on the display edge, let out an urgent squeak. “The dew point. It needs gentle moisture, not this absolute drenching.”

A thought, sharp and clear as a bell, cut the panic. The bloom did not need a flood; it needed a soft misty hug. Without a second’s hesitation she unclasped her own wolf-fur cloak, the garment she loved, a warm soft shield against the world, her ultimate comfort. Carefully, deliberately, she draped it over the Bloom, a cozy makeshift roof. Thick fibres soaked up the worst of the pounding, deflecting it from the delicate petals. Her own fur bristled, damp and icy cold, but the bloom beneath was safe, luminous petals shielded from the storm’s wild anger. Rain drummed a muffled roar on the cloak, distant thunder. Wet fur and damp earth filled the air, thick and strong. The rough cold soaked fabric against her skin was a stark reminder of discomfort—and, surprisingly, of a new strength blooming in her.

When the rain stopped, Madame Evangeline hurried in expecting disaster and found Sana dripping, remarkably steady, beside a Bloom whose petals unfurled with renewed radiance.

“Astonishing. Initiative. Remarkable composure.”

Sana smiled, small and genuine, a lightness unfamiliar. “It needed shelter from the worst of it. And the right kind of air.” The botany she could explain. The courage still felt like a delightful mystery.

Kit chirped happily from her shoulder, pure unadulterated relief. As the exhibition opened to murmurs of delighted wonder, Sana realized the frantic anxious voice that had always whispered doubts had finally quieted. Compliments about dazzling leadership and impressive calm no longer felt like a terrifying weight. They felt… nice. Visitors were not looking for perfect robots. They hoped for warmth, genuine care, a quiet dedication that was, to them, more enchanting than flawlessness. Sana, who had once frozen at the fear of not being good enough, found her footing not by pretending to be perfect, but by being present and brave, cloak still damp, bloom still hers.
characters: Sana (wolf trainee botanist), Kit (dormouse lab partner)
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
author: StoryGen Community
